**Patient Vignette: Mr. L.**

Mr. L. is a 75-year-old, South Eastern Asian man, a widower, who presents for an initial consultation at the urging of his adult daughter. He is a cybersecurity analyst, a role he has held for over three decades. He is precise, methodical, and speaks in a measured, deliberate tone, his hands often resting still on his knees. He describes his work as “finding the cracks before they break,” a philosophy he now applies to every waking moment.

The story he tells begins not in a server room, but in a hospital corridor, forty-two years ago. His son, then four years old, was diagnosed with a rare, aggressive form of leukemia. Mr. L. describes the moment of diagnosis not as a memory, but as a physical sensation that returns to him daily: a cold, metallic taste in his mouth, the sound of his own blood rushing in his ears, and the absolute, crystalline certainty that the world had just ended. He remembers the doctors’ words as a series of numbers—survival rates, white blood cell counts, chemotherapy cycles. He tried to treat it like a system breach: identify the vulnerability, isolate the threat, deploy a countermeasure. He researched relentlessly, learning the medical terminology, the drug protocols, the statistical probabilities. He believed that if he could just gather enough data, he could code a solution.

The treatment spanned three brutal years. His son endured rounds of chemo, spinal taps, and a bone marrow transplant. Mr. L. barely slept. He took a leave of absence from work, but his mind never stopped running diagnostics. He watched his son’s breathing at night, counting the seconds between each inhale and exhale. He memorized the pattern of the IV drip. He learned to read the subtle shifts in a nurse’s expression, the way a doctor’s shoulders might slump before delivering bad news. He became hypervigilant, scanning every room for hidden threats—a stray cough, a dropped toy, a flicker of fever.

His wife, he says, was the opposite. She held their son’s hand, sang to him, and cried openly. Mr. L. could not cry. He felt a terrible, frozen stillness inside, a kind of emotional paralysis he now recognizes as the beginning of his long, slow retreat. He told himself he was being strong, that he was the firewall protecting his family from chaos. In truth, he had disconnected from his own body, living entirely inside his own head.

His son survived. He is now a healthy, successful man with children of his own. But Mr. L. never returned from that hospital room. The world, for him, remains a place of imminent, catastrophic danger. He retired from his primary job, but took a contract role as a cybersecurity analyst for a small firm, a position that allows him to work from home. He spends his days in a dark, quiet office, monitoring network traffic for anomalies. He finds it calming, because the threats are logical, predictable, and can be neutralized with a line of code.

Outside of work, his life has narrowed to a set of rigid, self-imposed protocols. He checks the locks on his doors seven times before bed. He cannot sit with his back to a door. He avoids crowds, public transportation, and any environment where he cannot see all possible exits. He has not been to a hospital, even for a routine checkup, since his son’s last treatment. The smell of rubbing alcohol or antiseptic soap triggers a wave of nausea and a racing heart that he cannot control.

His wife died five years ago. He does not speak of her directly, but mentions her absence in the way he describes his daily routine. “I used to have coffee with her in the morning,” he says, his voice flat. “Now I just have coffee.” He has not dated, has few friends, and his primary social contact is his daughter, who calls every evening. He answers the phone on the first ring, every time, because he is always waiting for bad news.

He reports that he cannot remember the last time he felt joy. He does not feel sad, exactly; he feels hollow. He sleeps poorly, waking frequently, his mind replaying a loop of that hospital room: the beeping monitors, the smell of sterile gauze, the small, pale hand of his son. He avoids photographs from that period. He avoids thinking about it. But the past is not past; it is a live wire, humming just beneath the surface of his orderly, quiet life.
